Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: How to Run Locally

Guide to run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next locally.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is a new open-weight, 125B parameter MoE multimodal model from Qwen. Built on the new Qwen4 architecture, it supports a 256K context window. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next outperforms Claude-4.6-Opus (Max) and can run locally on devices with 32GB+ RAM/unified memory with no GPU VRAM required. To run the model, use our GGUFs via llama.cpp, Strata or Unsloth Desktop. Thank you Qwen for day zero access.

Nov 4: We're introducing our new Unsloth Dynamic v3.1 GGUFs, where 1-bit quant achieves 54.0% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 68.3% on Terminal Bench 2.1. Unsloth Qwen GGUFs result in 10-15% increased accuracy and 50% less token usage vs other quants of the same size.

Run Qwen3.8-FlashDownload Unsloth

Dynamic V3.1 Update (November 4th 2026)

We're releasing new Qwen3.8-Flash-Next GGUFs which using our new Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 (preview) algorithm which improves Unsloth quants on most benchmarks and is the best in class for it's size vs other providers. We previously showed how V3.1 for Dynamic V3.1 Update (November 2nd 2026) worked very well, and we're extending our new algorithms to Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

We ran agentic benchmarks including Terminal Bench 2.1, DeepSWE v1.1, Automation Bench v1.0.6, Aider Polyglot, and general benchmarks like LiveCodeBench v6, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, AIME25 and many others. Some highlights of our benchmarking process:

  • Benchmarks are noisy - we did 26.2B tokens of benchmarking - DeepSWE accounted for 18.1B tokens of the total budget followed by Terminal Bench (5.2B tokens).

  • temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, min_p 0, no presence or repetition penalty. preserve_thinking and xhigh reasoning.

  • We did the max 256K non YaRN context for all agentic benchmarks and 128K for generic non agentic benchmarks

  • We ran benchmarks multiple times including LiveCodeBench x3 times, HMMT and others 8-16x and agentic benchmarks multiple times.

Not only do you get extra accuracy, but Dynamic V3.1 bring thinking and token use down to match 95% of the full precision Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model. Result: up to 50% fewer token use, 7% faster + ~15% higher accuracy vs other quants of the same size.

Full benchmark results are provided as well, with the first plot being a percentage accuracy recovery from the baseline and averaged across all (not weighted). This approximately is a metric of what each quant retains in accuracy vs the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next baseline. We also ran KLD benchmarks as well vs our old V3 quants, and show a massive improvement as well.

All our metholodogies and graders, methods are discussed in Dynamic 3.1 GGUFs

Swap an engram you already downloaded

For example you want to switch out UD-Q6_K_XL with the lossless BF16 table. llama.cpp checks that each shard's split.no / split.count match its place in the set, so the table file has to be stamped for your quant first. set_split.py (in this folder, plain Python, no dependencies) changes those two header values in place in milliseconds; nothing else in the file changes.

⚙️ Usage Guide

Whether you run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a CPU with system RAM or on a GPU with VRAM may make relatively little difference. Its unique architecture allows inference using RAM or unified memory to achieve performance closer to that of GPU VRAM than is typical for other models. This makes it particularly well suited to Macs, NVIDIA DGX Spark systems, and other devices with large memory capacities.

You will need at least 75 GB of RAM or unified memory to run the model. Its smallest 1-bit quantized version is larger than usual because of new Ngram layers or per layer embeddings which is like a lookup table. However, this also means the quantization is less aggressive, allowing the model to retain more of its original accuracy than more heavily quantized models. You can also offload the PLE / Ngram layer to SSD and use mmap which allows less usage of CPU and GPU VRAM.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Requirements:

The smallest quant works on 32GB RAM so it's best to have a 32GB RAM/unified memory device. Table: Hardware requirements (units = total memory: RAM + VRAM, or unified memory)

Recommended Settings

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is a hybrid thinking model with different default settings for thinking and non-thinking modes. Extra high is enabled by default so if you want shorter thinking traces, you can adjust the thinking effort:

  • Context length = up to 262,144

  • Thinking Mode: temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=0.0, repetition_penalty=1.0

  • Instruct (or non-thinking) mode: temperature=0.7, top_p=0.80, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=1.5, repetition_penalty=1.0

💡 Thinking + Preserve Thinking

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has Preserve Thinking which leaves the thinking trace from the previous conversation. This increases the number of tokens you use, but could increase accuracy in continued conversations. Unsloth has 'Think' and Preserved Thinking toggles for Qwen3.8 (see right):

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next comes with support for reasoning_effort, which can be used to adjust reasoning depth and control cost. These toggles are automatically enabled in Unsloth:

  • xhigh (default): for complex tasks demanding thorough analysis

  • medium: balancing accuracy and speed

  • low: efficient reasoning optimizing for speed and cost

  • none

To change thinking / reasoning effort in unsloth run or llama-server, use --chat-template-kwargs '{"reasoning_effort":"medium"}'

If you're on Windows Powershell, use: --chat-template-kwargs "{\"reasoning_effort\":\"medium\"}"

Change medium to your desired reasoning level.

🦥 Run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in Unsloth

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next now is able to run in Unsloth Desktop, an open-source UI app for local AI. Unsloth automatically offloads to RAM and detects multiGPU setups. With Unsloth Desktop, you can run models locally on MacOS, Windows, Linux and:

  • Search, download, run GGUFs, MLX and safetensor models

  • Self-healing tool calling + web search

  • Code execution (Python, Bash)

  • Automatic inference parameter tuning (temp, top-p, etc.)

  • Fast CPU + GPU inference via MLX and llama.cpp

  • Train LLMs 2x faster with 70% less VRAM

For more information, you can view our Unsloth inference guide.

For example using Unsloth Desktop with the 397GB Qwen3.8 (-91% smaller) allows you to toggle thinking modes, allow inline canvas, web search and code execution and much more.

4

Serve Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with Unsloth API

You can use unsloth run command and serve Qwen3.8 via an API using llama-server runtime flags, including context sizing, GPU layers, threading, sampling, networking, and tool configuration. For more info see our API docs or unsloth start.

  • Train models: Fine-tune text, diffusion, embedding, and more

  • Generate media: Create and train images, video, TTS locally

MTP Guide

Qwen3.8-Flash can run with 1.3 to 1.7x faster inference via MTP (Multi-Token Prediction) with no accuracy degradation! MTP enables Qwen3.8-Flash to reach 170 tokens/s on 1x RTX 6000 PRO GPU compared to the 100 token baseline. MTP speeds up inference by letting a model predict multiple upcoming tokens at once instead of generating one token per step, and is especially effective on GPUs.

To run Qwen3.8-Flash with MTP, MTP is enabled by default in Unsloth Desktop or you can use our custom llama.cpp PR.

Gains are smaller on devices with lower memory bandwidth, such as older Macs. We created both shared MTP modules (excludes the embed_tokens and shares it with the main model) to save disk space, RAM and VRAM usage by around 1 to 2GB.

Further Quantization Analysis

We ran KLD for Qwen3.8-Flash quants, and show that 80% top-1 accuracy recovery is possible with 79% less disk space usage. The new architecture uses PLE / Ngrams, and these are not quantized that heavily (4-bit minimum) since they have random access pattern, and quantizing them heavily will damage the model.

import struct, sys
path, idx, cnt = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), int(sys.argv[3])
with open(path, "r+b") as f:
    head = f.read(1 << 24)
    for key, val in ((b"split.no", idx - 1), (b"split.count", cnt)):
        f.seek(head.index(struct.pack("<Q", len(key)) + key + struct.pack("<I", 2)) + len(key) + 12)
        f.write(struct.pack("<H", val))
# 1. UD-Q4_K_XL without its table shard (-00004-of-00004)
hf download unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF \
  --include "UD-Q4_K_XL/*" --exclude "UD-Q4_K_XL/*-00004-of-00004.gguf" --local-dir .

# 2. the Q8_0 table + the script
hf download unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF \
  --include "engram/*Q8_0*" "engram/set_split.py" --local-dir .

# 3. stamp it as shard 4 of 4 and put it in the table shard's place
python engram/set_split.py engram/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-engram-Q8_0.gguf_file 4 4
mv engram/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-engram-Q8_0.gguf_file \
   UD-Q4_K_XL/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q4_K_XL-00004-of-00004.gguf

# 4. run as usual
llama-server -m UD-Q4_K_XL/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q4_K_XL-00001-of-00004.gguf
# 1. get the table + the script
hf download unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF \
  --include "engram/*BF16*" "engram/set_split.py" --local-dir .

# 2. stamp it as shard 3 of 6 (UD-Q6_K_XL's table slot)
python engram/set_split.py engram/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-engram-BF16.gguf_file 3 6

# 3. keep the old table aside, then rename the new one to the table shard's name
mv UD-Q6_K_XL/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q6_K_XL-00003-of-00006.gguf UD-Q6_K_XL/engram-Q8_0.bak
mv engram/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-engram-BF16.gguf_file \
   UD-Q6_K_XL/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q6_K_XL-00003-of-00006.gguf

# 4. run as usual
llama-server -m UD-Q6_K_XL/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q6_K_XL-00001-of-00006.gguf
